- When sentiment is consistently low (≤0.3) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or add downward bias.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >75), model often overshoots and continues upward; cap forecast at +5–10% above peak or introduce early mean-reversion.
- If sentiment is high (≥0.7) and price is rising, model may overfit trend; apply smoothing or reduce forecast slope to avoid overcorrection.
- When true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of decline after peak), model often fails to adjust; add lagged mean-reversion term or reduce forecast momentum.
- If model forecast is flat or rising slowly but true outcome shows volatility, sentiment history should trigger early volatility adjustment (e.g., ±2–3% buffer around forecast).
- For 30-day horizon, model often underestimates volatility in early days after a spike; increase forecast variance or add sentiment-weighted volatility multiplier.
